analysis.one_liner: Imposes uniform federal rules that make product-injury lawsuits harder to win, shorter-lived, and smaller.
analysis.headline: Backed by 34 senators including 8 Democrats, the bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee in June 1990 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never came up for a vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the states' differing product liability rules with a single federal scheme tilted toward defendants. Lawsuits would face a two-year filing deadline, punitive damages would require proof of "conscious, flagrant indifference" to safety, makers of FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified aircraft would be immune from punitive damages, and awards would shrink through workers' compensation offsets and limits on holding one defendant responsible for another's share of pain-and-suffering damages. The Commerce Committee reported it favorably in June 1990 and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never came up for a vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, product sellers, and liability insurers gain if the bill passes: one uniform federal liability scheme replaces 50 differing state regimes, claims face a two-year deadline, punitive damages require proof of "conscious, flagrant indifference" by clear and convincing evidence, makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices and FAA-certificated aircraft are shielded from punitive damages entirely, and damage awards shrink through workers' compensation offsets and limits on shared liability.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the varying product liability laws of the 50 states with one uniform federal set of rules, superseding state provisions that give injured people more ways to recover.

Allows punitive damages only if the claimant proves by clear and convincing evidence that the harm resulted from the manufacturer's or seller's 'conscious, flagrant indifference' to safety — a far higher bar than most state law imposes.

Bars punitive damages entirely against makers of FDA-approved drugs and medical devices and FAA-certificated aircraft, unless the defendant withheld or misrepresented material information from the agency.
Cuts off any claim not filed within two years of discovering the harm, and bars suits over business equipment more than 25 years after delivery.
Limits sellers who did not make the product to narrow negligence and express-warranty claims, generally shielding them from liability for defects they did not create.

Makes each defendant pay only its own proportional share of pain-and-suffering damages rather than the full award, and reduces awards by the workers' compensation benefits the injured worker received or is owed.

Gives manufacturers and sellers a complete defense when the injured person was intoxicated and more than 50 percent responsible for the event, and adds expedited settlement and alternative dispute resolution procedures to resolve cases faster.

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products bear the cost: shorter filing deadlines, a much higher bar for punitive damages, awards reduced by workers' compensation benefits, no joint liability for pain and suffering when one defendant cannot pay its share, and a near-complete liability shield for sellers who did not make the product.

drawbacks.text: An injured person would have at most two years from discovery to sue, regardless of the longer deadlines many states allow, and the bill would shorten existing exposure periods with only a one-year grace window for claims already cut off.

Punitive damages would require proof of 'conscious, flagrant indifference' by clear and convincing evidence, ruling out penalties for reckless corporate conduct that falls short of that standard, and makers of FDA-approved drugs and devices would be immune from punitive damages altogether.
Each defendant would pay only its proportional share of pain-and-suffering damages, so if a co-defendant cannot pay its share, the injured person absorbs the loss.

Damages would be reduced by the full amount of workers' compensation benefits received or owed, and workers generally could not sue their employers, leaving many injured workers with only the lower workers' compensation recovery.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's supporters argued for predictability: one national liability standard instead of 50 state regimes, faster settlements, and lower litigation costs that defenders said would show up in consumer prices. Those benefits accrue mainly to manufacturers, sellers, and their insurers. The costs fall on people hurt by defective products — shorter deadlines, a punitive damages standard most cases could never meet, immunity for FDA-approved drugs and certified aircraft, awards reduced by workers' compensation, and no joint liability when a co-defendant cannot pay. The bill does preserve environmental claims, sovereign immunity, and a fallback against sellers when the manufacturer cannot be sued, but the pattern is clear: nearly every new restriction runs in one direction, against claimants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Commerce Committee, sat on the Senate's calendar of pending business, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Kasten introduced the bill on July 25, 1989 with 19 original cosponsors from both parties; it eventually drew 34 cosponsors, including 8 of the Senate's 55 Democrats and 26 of its 45 Republicans.
The Commerce Committee's Consumer Subcommittee held hearings in February, April, and May 1990, and the full committee reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment on June 19, 1990.

The Senate then referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee for up to 60 days; Judiciary held hearings on July 31, 1990 and was discharged on August 30, and the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 807.
The bill never received a Senate floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers, product sellers, and liability insurers are better off because the bill died: the federal law that would have shortened filing deadlines, raised the punitive damages bar, preempted state rules favorable to injured people, and capped their exposure never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Product makers, sellers, and liability insurers

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote was ever held; among the 34 cosponsors, Republicans joined at a far higher rate (26 of 45) than Democrats (8 of 55), and the Democratic Senate leadership never brought the bill to the floor.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers (including drug, device, and aircraft makers)
industries.note: The bill hands manufacturers a uniform federal shield: a two-year filing deadline, a near-unattainable punitive damages standard, immunity from punitive damages for FDA-approved drugs and devices and FAA-certificated aircraft, and reduced exposure through workers' compensation offsets and several liability. Their gain comes directly out of the recovery available to people hurt by their products.

Retailers, distributors, and others who sell but do not make products would generally escape liability for defective goods, closing a common route by which injured buyers reached a solvent defendant. The bill preserves a fallback only when the manufacturer cannot be sued or a judgment against it enforced.
Tighter liability rules, shorter deadlines, and caps on punitive and joint liability translate directly into fewer and smaller payouts on liability policies.

Shorter deadlines, stricter proof standards, and smaller, less collectible awards would cut the volume and value of contingency-fee injury cases. In this bill the plaintiffs' bar's interest ran alongside injured consumers'.
